hi, my tomato plants are acting weird. the leaves at the bottom are turning yellow but the ones at the top look okay. what do you think is going on and how can i fix the soil?

Yellowing lower leaves on tomatoes is a classic sign of nitrogen deficiency — the plant pulls nitrogen from older leaves to feed new growth at the top. It can also indicate overwatering or early blight, but nitrogen is the most common culprit, especially if the yellowing is uniform rather than spotted.

To fix the soil, work in some compost or aged manure, or apply a balanced fertilizer (something like 5-10-5 or 10-10-10) around the base. Water deeply but less frequently — tomatoes prefer a good soak once or twice a week over daily sprinkles. thanks for the advice. i tried adding some compost like you said but i'm worried something might be eating the nutrients before the plants can get them. is there anything else i should check for that might be stripping the soil? maybe pests or something?

Good instinct to check — though in most cases it's not pests literally eating soil nutrients, but there are a few things worth ruling out. Root-feeding pests like grubs, cutworms, or root-knot nematodes can damage roots so the plant can't take up nutrients properly, even if the soil is rich. Gently dig around the base of a plant and look for white C-shaped grubs, chewed or swollen/knotted roots, or wilting despite moist soil.

Also check the simpler stuff first: soil pH. If it's outside the 6.0–6.8 range, tomatoes can't absorb nitrogen even when it's present — a cheap soil test kit will tell you. Exactly — "locked up" is a great way to put it. Soil pH controls whether nutrients are chemically available for roots to absorb. When pH drifts too high (alkaline) or too low (acidic), nutrients like nitrogen, phosphorus, and iron can be present in the soil but chemically bound in forms the roots simply can't take up. The plant shows deficiency symptoms even though a soil test would say the nutrients are there.

That's why pH is worth checking before adding more fertilizer — you could keep pouring nutrients into locked soil and the plant still starves. If your test shows pH above 7, elemental sulfur or acidic organic matter like pine needles or peat moss can bring it down; below 6, garden lime raises it.
